reasoning: All substantive file reviews across all three reports found the package safe. The PKGBUILD contains only standard variable assignments at top-level with no command substitution or network operations during sourcing. The build/package functions use standard patterns (git submodule sync, go build, install commands). Shell completion scripts (bash, fish, zsh) are standard Cobra-generated files where eval usage is expected and only invokes the package's own binary. Desktop entries, systemd service, and install hook are all standard and benign. The inconclusive verdicts in Reports 1 and 2 were caused by tool errors (API failures, empty LLM responses), not by substantive security concerns. Report 3 (advisory) successfully reviewed all files including those that failed in other reports, confirming safety.
disagreement_analysis: No substantive disagreement exists. Reports 1 and 2 returned inconclusive due to tool errors (HTTP 400 API failures for PKGBUILD and completions.fish in Report 1; empty LLM response for completions.zsh in Report 2), not due to security findings. Report 3 (advisory) successfully reviewed all files and found them safe. The files that failed in one report were successfully reviewed in others, providing complete coverage.
coverage_issues: Report 1: PKGBUILD and completions.fish failed with HTTP 400 API errors
Report 2: completions.zsh failed with empty LLM response
learnings: Tool errors (API failures, empty responses) should not block a safe verdict when other reports provide complete coverage of the same files
Cross-report file coverage analysis can compensate for individual report failures - if a file failed in one report but succeeded in another, the successful review should count
Standard Cobra-generated completion scripts with eval are correctly identified as safe when the eval only invokes the package's own binary with user-typed arguments
Initial PKGBUILD audits that pass (checking top-level scope only) provide partial but valuable signal even when full review fails
